paras: The threats against exodus leader Samuel L. Perry were a series of warnings and a search by armed horsemen aimed at Perry, a Black teacher and organizer, at Lagrange, Lenoir County, North Carolina, in late 1879, after he led Black emigrants from the state to Indiana. No attack on him is reported; the episode became public in November 1880, when Perry's wife and mother described it under oath in Washington while he fought extradition to North Carolina on a forgery charge.

In 1879 he organized a secret emigration society, and he said the Goldsboro Messenger 'advocated putting him out of the way' once his leadership became known. White papers of the time described him as 'a notorious negro' and 'an agitator' who had misled the emigrants. He and P. C. Williams left with a party of emigrants on September 15, 1879, and went on to Indianapolis and Greencastle.

When Perry wrote ahead that he was returning, he received letters warning him not to come, and he left the train before it reached the Lagrange depot. He stayed about twenty days but never at his own home, moved between houses kept secret, and said at least 20 armed men guarded him because he believed he would be murdered.

His wife, named by the National Republican as Jennie Perry, testified that 'men on horseback called at the house and demanded him' and left when they did not find him. She said a white woman told her of a plan to capture her husband and urged that he leave, and that others told her he 'would be killed if caught'; his mother, Catherine Perry, confirmed this account. In January 1880 his brother Rufus wrote him not to come back, and Jerry Williams wrote that he could name 20 white men who would kill Perry for getting up the exodus.

No arrest or prosecution of the horsemen appears in the coverage. Instead, on October 25, 1880, Perry was arrested in Washington on a requisition from North Carolina charging him and his brother Aaron E. Perry with forging a $45 school order in Lenoir County. His counsel argued that the charge was political revenge and that he 'will be destroyed' if returned, and Richard T. Greener said the state's agent shared a name with a man accused of killing nine Black men and throwing them into the Neuse River.

Chief Justice Cartter ordered Perry surrendered on October 29, but Perry at once sought habeas corpus, swearing he would be 'in great bodily danger' in North Carolina. The agent, George K. Bagby, testified that there was no vindictiveness toward Perry over the exodus 'now, whatever there may have been.' On November 10, Judge Wylie doubted that Perry had proved he would be in danger, but noted that feeling against him had been hostile and discharged him because the indictment was defective and the 'moral atmosphere' of the case suspicious. The General Term affirmed the discharge on July 6, 1881, and North Carolina gave notice of appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court; no later outcome was found.

Almost all coverage came from Washington, and the threats themselves appeared only in the Evening Star's and National Republican's reports of the November 5 hearing. The National Republican headlined the arrest 'A Sequel to the Exodus' and 'How North Carolina Democrats are Trying to Get Even,' and a Chicago Tribune dispatch called it 'an attempt at bulldozing.' The Alexandria Gazette's correspondent instead called Perry 'the exodus negro forger' whom the government was shielding.

The wire report of the November 6 hearing, which ran in St. Paul under 'Much Ado About a Black Forger' and in Chicago as 'The Exodus Leader in the Hands of the Democrats,' mentioned the Ku-Klux exchange but not the testimony about the horsemen. No Black-press or North Carolina account of the threats was found.

Perry's side said he faced murder if returned, while Bagby and North Carolina's counsel denied any danger or political motive, and Judge Wylie found the danger not proved. Reports also differed on the charge itself, which the Washington papers described as a forged $45 school order and the wire as raising a teacher's certificate from $15 to $45.

reader.title: Threats against exodus leader Samuel L. Perry
bases: Sworn testimony reported in Washington describes armed horsemen seeking Perry at his home, a plan to capture him, and threats that he would be killed, with no attack carried out (A25, A26, A27).

No one was killed or injured; Perry's wife and mother testified that unnamed men on horseback sought him and that he would be killed if caught, which is a threat of lynching, not a lynching (A26, A27).

Every account of the horsemen and threats comes from Perry, his wife and mother, and letters they produced at one habeas corpus hearing; the Evening Star and National Republican report the same testimony, and Judge Wylie accepted that feeling against Perry had been hostile but doubted the danger case had been made out (A25, A26, A27, A34).

framing.detail: The National Republican headlined 'A Sequel to the Exodus. How North Carolina Democrats are Trying to Get Even' and called the case political persecution.
A Chicago Tribune special dispatch called the arrest 'very much like an attempt at bulldozing'.
The Alexandria Gazette's Washington correspondent called Perry 'the exodus negro forger' and accused the government of shielding a criminal.
The Nov. 6 wire report ran as 'Much Ado About a Black Forger' in St. Paul and as 'The Exodus Leader in the Hands of the Democrats' in Chicago.
The Evening Star covered each hearing under 'The Alleged Exodus Leader' with long verbatim exchanges.
In 1879 the New York Herald's Goldsboro letter called Perry 'a notorious negro' who profited from 'exodus fever'.
